30.0.big: Cells need oxygen for cellular respiration and must get rid of carbon dioxide. The respiratory system handles that swap.
points: Gas exchange always works by diffusion, from high partial pressure to low.

30.1.big: Small or flat animals exchange gas straight through their surface. Bigger animals need gills, tracheal tubes or lungs.
points: Direct diffusion works for tiny or thin organisms. Earthworms and frogs also use moist skin. Fish use gills.
Insects use a tracheal system: tubes running from body openings (spiracles) straight to cells.

The human path: nasal cavity (warms, humidifies and filters air) → pharynx → larynx (voice box) → trachea → primary bronchus (one per lung) → smaller bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs → alveoli.
Alveoli are tiny thin-walled sacs wrapped in capillaries: a huge surface area (about 75 m²) for diffusion.
Protection: hair and mucus (made from mucin) trap particulate matter, and cilia sweep it up and out.

30.2.big: Oxygen and CO₂ move by diffusion down their partial pressure gradients: air → alveoli → blood → tissues, and back for CO₂.
points: Partial pressure = each gas's share of the total air pressure. Air in the alveoli has less O₂ than outside air because it's mixed with leftover air and water vapor, and O₂ is constantly diffusing into the blood.
In the lungs, O₂ is higher in the alveoli than in the venous blood arriving, so it moves in. In tissues, O₂ is higher in arterial blood than in cells, so it moves out. CO₂ goes the opposite way.

Spirometry measures lung volumes: tidal volume (TV) (a normal breath), inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) (extra you can breathe in), expiratory reserve volume (ERV) (extra you can breathe out), residual volume (RV) (always left in the lungs).
Lung capacities are sums: vital capacity (VC) = TV + IRV + ERV, total lung capacity (TLC) = all four, inspiratory capacity (IC) = TV + IRV, functional residual capacity (FRC) = ERV + RV.

FEV1/FVC ratio: how much of your functional vital capacity (FVC) you can blow out in 1 second (forced expiratory volume (FEV)). High ratio = stiff lungs (fibrosis). Low ratio = blocked airways (asthma).
The respiratory quotient (RQ) compares CO₂ made to O₂ used, and it depends on the food being burned.

30.3.big: Breathing works by changing chest volume: bigger chest = lower pressure = air rushes in.
points: Inhale: the diaphragm contracts and moves down, and the intercostal muscles lift the ribs, so pressure in the intrapleural space drops and air flows in. Exhale (at rest): the muscles relax and the elastic recoil of the lungs pushes air out.
Each lung is wrapped in a two-layer pleura. Inflamed pleura (pleurisy) makes breathing painful.
Surfactant coats the alveoli and lowers surface tension so they don't collapse. Premature babies lacking it get respiratory distress syndrome.

Work of breathing: compliance = how easily the lungs stretch (elastic work). Resistance = how hard air is to push through the airways (flow-resistive work). Restrictive disease (like fibrosis) lowers compliance. Obstructive disease (like asthma or swollen airways) raises resistance.
Respiratory rate × air per breath sets alveolar ventilation. You can breathe fast and shallow or slow and deep.

Dead space = air that doesn't reach working alveoli. Anatomical dead space = the airways themselves. Physiological dead space = alveoli that don't exchange gas (for example, no blood flow). A ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch means air and blood flow don't match; the body adjusts with recruitment (opening more capillaries). Standing up, the top of the lung has the highest V/Q.

30.4.big: Hemoglobin in red blood cells carries most oxygen. Most CO₂ travels as bicarbonate.
points: Each hemoglobin has four heme groups (iron), so it carries up to 4 O₂. Binding is cooperative: once one O₂ binds, the rest bind more easily (the S-shaped oxygen dissociation curve). This sets blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
The curve shifts right (Hb lets go of O₂ more easily) with more CO₂, lower pH, and higher temperature: exactly what working muscles need. It shifts left with the opposite.
Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin far more tightly than O₂. Treatment is 100% oxygen to push it off.
Blood disorders: sickle cell anemia (misshapen red blood cells carry O₂ poorly) and thalassemia (not enough working hemoglobin).

CO₂ transport: about 70% as bicarbonate, made by carbonic anhydrase (CA) in red cells (CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻). About 20% binds hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin, and about 10% dissolves in plasma.
Chloride shift: bicarbonate leaves the red cell into the plasma and chloride comes in to balance the charge. This bicarbonate buffer system also keeps blood pH steady.
30.4.tip: Exercising muscle is hot, acidic and full of CO₂, which all make hemoglobin drop off more oxygen right where it's needed.

1.why: Its main job is to supply oxygen (and remove CO₂, not supply it).

2.why: Nose → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

3.why: Warming and humidifying air protects the trachea and lungs from damage.

5.why: IRV = the extra air you can breathe in after a normal breath.

6.why: TLC = RV + ERV + TV + IRV (all four volumes).

7.why: Oxygen is constantly diffusing out of the alveoli into the blood, and the air there is mixed with water vapor, so its O₂ share is lower.

8.why: Less O₂ in the air = a smaller pressure difference = slower diffusion into the blood.

9.why: Intercostals contract to inhale and relax to exhale (at rest).

10.why: Without the diaphragm contracting, chest pressure won't drop, so air won't flow in.

11.why: Restrictive diseases make lungs stiffer: lower compliance.

12.why: Narrower airways = more resistance to air flow.

13.why: Physiological dead space = alveoli that aren't exchanging gas, for example because their capillaries get no blood.

14.why: The body compensates: too little ventilation → breathe faster and deeper. Too much → slower and shallower.

15.why: Elastic recoil = the stretched lung pushing back inward, which helps exhale.

16.why: Low pH decreases hemoglobin's grip on oxygen, so it releases more.

17.why: Lower temperature makes hemoglobin hold oxygen tighter. The others help release it.

19.why: Swapping chloride in lets bicarbonate move out into the plasma to be carried.

20.why: Grape-like sacs give a huge surface area.

21.why: Hair and mucus trap particles, and the nasal cavity warms the air.

23.why: FEV1/FVC = forced expiratory volume in 1 s over forced vital capacity. Fibrosis makes lungs stiff, so the ratio rises.

24.why: O₂ is lower in venous blood than in alveolar air (so it loads) and higher in arterial blood than in tissues (so it unloads).

25.why: Restrictive disease (stiff lungs) raises the ratio. Increased resistance (obstruction) lowers it.

26.why: Mammals expand the chest, creating negative pressure that pulls air in. Frogs push air in.

27.why: At the same 40 cm H₂O, the lungs without surfactant hold only about half the volume.

28.why: At the top of the lung, blood flow is low compared with air: the highest V/Q.

29.why: Flooding with O₂ pushes CO off hemoglobin. CO₂ wouldn't help because O₂ binds hemoglobin more strongly than CO₂.

30.why: Without carbonic anhydrase, CO₂ isn't turned into bicarbonate, so the blood carries only a small fraction of it.

31.why: A genetic disease with sickle-shaped red cells that carry less oxygen.

32.why: A huge single cell must make diffusion across its membrane more efficient.

33.why: The lines go up: bigger animals have bigger respiratory surfaces.

34.why: Air comes in through the bronchiole (inhaled air), and the pulmonary artery brings blood from the heart. (The A/B labels aren't printed on the book's figure.)

35.why: The tube goes in below the blockage to bypass it, so the injury is above the site.

36.why: Equal O₂ in cell and blood means no diffusion. The body would speed up the heart to bring more oxygen.

37.why: In tissues, O₂ moves from the high-O₂ RBC into the low-O₂ body cell. CO₂ moves from the high-CO₂ cell into the RBC.

38.why: As hemoglobin nears full, there are fewer open binding sites, so extra O₂ adds less: the curve flattens.

39.why: Left shift (holds O₂ tighter) comes from less CO₂, higher pH, lower temperature.

40.why: More CO₂ lowers pH, so hemoglobin lets go more easily: the curve shifts right.
